nameStory: The spotted redshank gets its name from the distinctive speckled pattern on its plumage and its bright reddish-orange legs that really stand out against mudflats and shallow water. The word 'shank' refers to the lower part of a bird's leg, and this species shows off those colorful shanks like they're wearing bright red boots!
description: The spotted redshank is a medium-sized shorebird that's an extremely rare visitor to New England waters. This elegant wader has long, bright red-orange legs and a long, straight bill that's perfect for probing in shallow water and mud. In breeding plumage, it's almost entirely dark with white spots, while in winter it becomes much paler gray above and white below. These birds are built for wading, standing about the size of a small duck but much more slender.

idTips.label: Bright Red Legs
idTips.description: The most striking feature - vivid reddish-orange legs that look like they've been dipped in bright paint, much more intense than the yellow legs of similar shorebirds

idTips.label: Long Straight Bill
idTips.description: A needle-straight, dark bill that's longer than the head, with a slightly reddish base that you can see up close - feels rigid and pointed if you were to touch a museum specimen

idTips.label: Dark Breeding Plumage
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, appears almost coal-black with white spots scattered across like stars, creating a striking speckled pattern that catches the eye

idTips.label: Pale Winter Plumage
idTips.description: In fall and winter, transforms to soft gray above and clean white below, with a distinctive white eyebrow stripe that gives it an alert expression

idTips.label: Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Feeds by walking deliberately through shallow water, probing and sweeping its bill side to side like it's painting with a brush, often wading deeper than most sandpipers

habitat: In New England, spotted redshanks would most likely appear at coastal mudflats, salt marshes, and shallow tidal pools along the Atlantic shore. They prefer areas where they can wade in ankle-deep water with soft, muddy bottoms rich in marine worms and small crustaceans. Look for them at famous birding spots like Plum Island or other protected coastal areas where rare shorebirds occasionally turn up.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare, but if seen would likely be in striking dark breeding plumage with bright white spots. May migration would be the most likely time for a vagrant to appear.
seasonality.summer: Virtually absent from New England during breeding season, as they nest in the far northern regions of Scandinavia and northern Asia thousands of miles away.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration offers the best chance of spotting one, though still extraordinarily rare. Birds would be molting from dark breeding plumage to pale winter colors.
seasonality.winter: Unlikely to overwinter in New England's harsh climate, as they typically continue south to tropical regions or southern Europe for the winter months.

funFact: Only one spotted redshank has ever been officially recorded in all of New England - making it rarer here than finding a four-leaf clover in your backyard, and if you saw one, you'd instantly become part of a very exclusive club of New England birders!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with the much more common Greater Yellowlegs, but remember 'red legs, not yellow legs' - the spotted redshank's bright orange-red legs are unmistakable compared to the yellowlegs' bright yellow ones. In winter plumage, the spotted redshank is also cleaner white below with less streaking.
contextualKnowledge: This is what birders call a 'vagrant' - a bird that has wandered far outside its normal range, likely blown off course during migration. The single New England record makes this a 'mega-rarity' that would draw birders from hundreds of miles away if one appeared.
compareHints: Compared to its New England cousins, the spotted redshank has the brightest colored legs - much more vivid red-orange than the yellow of both yellowlegs species. It's also longer-legged and more elegant than the stocky Willet, and much larger than the delicate Solitary Sandpiper. The bill is straighter and longer proportionally than any of these related species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tringa relatives, Greater Yellowlegs is larger than Lesser Yellowlegs and Solitary Sandpiper, with brighter yellow legs than either.
Among its Tringa relatives, the willet dwarfs both greater and lesser yellowlegs with its robust build and lacks their bright yellow legs entirely.
Compared to its Tringa cousins, the Solitary Sandpiper is smaller than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs with much darker, greenish legs instead of bright yellow ones.
Compared to its close relative the Greater Yellowlegs, the Lesser is noticeably smaller with a shorter, always-straight bill.
Wood Sandpiper is much smaller and more delicate than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs, with proportionally shorter legs and bill.
Compared to its New England relatives in the same genus, the Common Redshank is smaller than Greater Yellowlegs but similar in size to Lesser Yellowlegs, though much stockier in build.
